lessons.title: 01 · From discrete symmetry to continuous symmetry
lessons.summary: First ask whether the parameters can change continuously, and then distinguish the order of the group, the dimension of the group and the size of the matrix.
objectives: Identify the difference between point group , space group and continuous rotation
Use the unit circle to understand U(1)
Avoid equating "there are infinitely many elements" with "continuous group"

sections.title: What rotations are allowed for a square?
paragraphs: Considering only proper in-plane rotations, a square allows 0°,90°,180°,270°, forming the four-element group C₄. An ideal disk permits every angle, forming SO(2). Both obey group multiplication rules, but the latter permits continuous motion in angle from the identity.

crystal point group is a finite group; three-dimensional space group contains infinite lattice translations and is still a discrete group. n in translation n a can only be an integer, not 0.001 arbitrarily. Therefore "infinite" is not enough to describe "continuous". Here we focus on learning the continuous Lie group of positive dimensions; mathematically the discrete group can also be regarded as zero-dimensional Lie group .

sections.title: U(1): One angle forms a circle
paragraphs: The complex number e^(iφ) has modulus 1. Multiplication of two such numbers remains on the unit circle; multiplication corresponds to the addition of angles. φ and φ+2π are the same group elements, so the overall space where the parameters are located is a circle, not a straight line without end to end.

Lie group has both group structure and smooth manifold structure, and both multiplication and inversion are smooth. The real dimension of U(1) is 1, which means that a continuous real parameter is required locally; it does not have only one element. SO(2) and U(1) are isomorphic, but one can act on real plane coordinates, and the other is often written as complex phase.

example.title: Think of C₄ as four points in U(1)
steps: Take r=e^(iπ/2)=i and write the identity element as 1.
Successive multiplication gives 1, r=i, r²=−1 and r³=−i; one more multiplication by r gives r⁴=1.
falls back into these four points, so they form a subgroup.
e^(iπ/4) belongs to U(1) but not to these four points. Allowing it within U(1) does not give the square a 45° symmetry.
example.result: C₄ is a finite subgroup of U(1); a continuous group can contain discrete subgroups.

lessons.pitfall: space group contains infinite translations, and still does not allow any small translations; do not use the number of elements instead of continuity judgment.

quiz.explanation: The dimension describes the number of local parameters of the group itself, which is different from the number of elements of the group and the dimension of the vector space specifically represented.

lessons.title: 02 · Why use unitary matrix ?
lessons.summary: Understand the name SU(n) through complex moduli, conjugate transposes, and probability conservation.
objectives: Computes the norm of a complex vector and conjugate transpose
distinguishes between U(n) and SU(n)
Understand that preserving the norm does not mean preserving the probability of each component

sections.title: length of complex amplitude
paragraphs: Write a two-level state as ψ=(a,b)ᵀ with complex amplitudes a,b. Normalization requires |a|²+|b|²=1; in the chosen basis, measurement probabilities are |a|² and |b|². Complex conjugation sends i to −i; conjugate transpose † additionally exchanges rows and columns.

If U†U=I, then the norm of ψ′=Uψ is still 1 after transformation. U can mix different components, so the probability of an individual outcome can change; what remains constant is the total probability and the inner product between the vectors.

sections.title: special is an additional determinant condition
paragraphs: U(n) consists of all n×n unitary matrices. SU(n) additionally requires det U=1; S means special and U unitary. n counts complex-vector components in the fundamental representation, not the dimension of the group.

A unitary matrix’s determinant has modulus 1 but may carry a phase. Requiring the determinant to equal exactly 1 is an additional restriction. Numerical calculations report unitarity and determinant errors; small floating-point errors are not new physical effects.
sections.formula:
SU(n) = {U∈ℂⁿˣⁿ : U†U=I and det U=1}
U_z(θ) = diag(e^(−iθ/2), e^(iθ/2))

example.title: checks whether a matrix belongs to SU(2)
steps: Let U=diag(e^(−iπ/4),e^(iπ/4)), the modulus of both terms is 1.
conjugate transpose is U†=diag(e^(iπ/4),e^(−iπ/4)), so U†U=I.
is the product of two terms e^(−iπ/4)e^(iπ/4)=1, so U∈SU(2).
Compare V=diag(i,1): V†V=I, but det V=i, so V∈U(2) and V∉SU(2).
example.result: Checking SU(n) must check both unitarity and determinant; verifying probability conservation is not enough.

lessons.pitfall: † is not just a transpose; omitting complex conjugation will miscalculate the unitarity check. SU(n) also does not require every matrix element to be a real number.

quiz.question: V=diag(i,1) belong to?
choices: SU(2)
U(2), but not SU(2)
Neither
quiz.explanation: V†V=I, so it is unitary matrix ; det V=i≠1 does not meet the additional requirements of special.

choices: The probability of each component remains unchanged respectively

The total probability and inner product remain unchanged
quiz.explanation: Unitarity preserves norms and inner products while allowing probabilities to redistribute among basis states.

lessons.title: 03 · Generators and commutators: understand groups through small changes
lessons.summary: Break the finite transformation into many small changes and understand why the order of operations is important.
objectives: Identify generator from expansion near the identity matrix
Calculation [A,B]=AB−BA
distinguishes Hermitian generator from anti-Hermitian Lie algebra in mathematics

sections.title: matrix exponential connection local and finite transformation
paragraphs: This class uses common conventions in physics: T is Hermitian generator , U(θ)=exp(−iθT). When θ is small, U≈I−iθT;T specifies the direction in which to initially leave the identity element. For SU(n), T is also traceless, so det exp(−iθT)=exp(−iθ Tr T)=1.

The real Lie algebra su(n) consists of traceless anti-Hermitian matrices X, with X=−iT here. Hermitian matrices are not closed under ordinary matrix commutators: the commutator of two Hermitian matrices is anti-Hermitian, which is why physics formulas explicitly contain i.

sections.title: Should you do A or B first?
paragraphs: The commutator [A,B]=AB−BA compares the two operation orders. For column vectors, ABψ applies B first, then A. If [A,B]=0, exponentials of that generator pair commute as well; in general, exp(A)exp(B) cannot be combined directly into exp(A+B).

The interactive experiment compares two generator pairs: SU(2) Tx and Ty do not commute, while SU(3) T3 and T8 do. A zero commutator means no order dependence for that pair, not that the whole group is Abelian.

example.title: Calculate an SU(2) commutator directly
steps: Matrix multiplication gives σxσy=iσz, swapping the order gives σyσx=−iσz.

Because Ta=σa/2, divide both sides by 4: [Tx,Ty]=(i/2)σz=iTz.
example.result: The difference between generator orders is still expressible in terms of generators, provided i and normalization factors are retained.

lessons.title: 04 · SU(2), Pauli matrix and two-component spinor
lessons.summary: A spinor has two complex components, while rotations have three generators. The Bloch sphere connects these descriptions.
objectives: recognizes three Pauli matrices
Compute finite rotation of spin 1/2
Computes Bloch vector from two-component state

sections.title: Two components, three directions of rotation
paragraphs: The SU(2) fundamental representation acts on ψ=(a,b)ᵀ∈ℂ². Spin-1/2 angular momentum is Sa=ℏσa/2; the course separates ℏ and uses dimensionless generators Ta=σa/2. The group dimension is 3, while the fundamental-representation dimension is 2: these are different concepts.

around the unit axis n can be directly calculated by (n·σ)²=I as the exponent: even powers merge into cosine, and odd powers merge into sine. θ here is the right-hand active rotation angle, and what changes is the state, not the coordinate base.

sections.title: The Bloch sphere displays the expectation-value direction
paragraphs: A normalized pure state has unit Bloch vector r=(⟨σx⟩,⟨σy⟩,⟨σz⟩). Spin expectation is ⟨S⟩=(ℏ/2)r. |↑z⟩=(1,0)ᵀ lies at the north pole, while (1,1)ᵀ/√2 points along +x.

Bloch diagram does not preserve the overall phase: ψ and e^(iχ)ψ correspond to the same point. The experiment also gives the complex amplitude and the overlap with the initial state, making it easy to distinguish between "the same arrows" and "the same state vectors". This experiment only operates the normalized pure state; generally the mixed state is located inside the Bloch sphere.

example.title: rotates the +z spin 90° around the y-axis
steps: initial state ψ₀=(1,0)ᵀ, take n=(0,1,0), θ=π/2.
Applying the matrix to the initial state gives ψ₁=(1,1)ᵀ/√2, with both z-basis probabilities 1/2.
Substitution into the Bloch formula gives r=(1,0,0), consistent with rotating +z toward +x by the right-hand rule.
example.result: state become 1/2, but the total probability remains 1; the three-dimensional direction comes from the expected value of the spinor.

lessons.pitfall: The Bloch-sphere arrow is a spin expectation, not an electron’s trajectory spinning as a small ball or an atom’s coordinate in a cell.

quiz.question: actively rotates π/2 around the y-axis, what direction does the Bloch vector of |↑z⟩ point?
choices: +x
−x
+z
quiz.explanation: This course uses U=exp(−iθσy/2), giving (1,1)/√2 and hence +x. Reversing the exponent’s sign reverses the active rotation.

choices: 2 and 3
3 and 2

quiz.explanation: three independent real entities generator correspond to group dimension 3; the basic representation acts on a two-component complex vector with dimension 2.

lessons.title: 05 · 2π vs. 4π: Why double group ?
lessons.summary: The same three-dimensional positive rotation corresponds to two SU(2) elements; when the negative sign is meaningful, it depends on the object of comparison.
objectives: understands the dual coverage of SU(2)→SO(3)
distinguishes between overall phase and relative phase
connects continuous rotation with crystal double group and magnetic groups

sections.title: The same three-dimensional arrow may correspond to spinors differing by a minus sign
paragraphs: Define the rotated vector through U(r·σ)U† to obtain R(U)∈SO(3). Replacing U by −U cancels the two minus signs and leaves R unchanged. Every three-dimensional proper rotation therefore has two preimages ±U, with kernel {I,−I}.

Substituting into the rotation formula, we know that U(2π)=−I, and U(4π)=I. The former makes the entire two-component vector negative, but the Bloch vector remains unchanged. The Lie algebra of su(2) and so(3) are isomorphic, which does not mean that SU(2) and SO(3) are the same global group.

sections.title: The overall negative sign alone is invisible, and the relative negative signs of the two paths can interfere.
paragraphs: For isolated pure states, ψ and −ψ give the same measurement probability and represent the same quantum state ray. You can't just look at the spin measurements and declare the discovery of this global negative sign.

If the path is coherently divided into branches a and b, and only 2π rotation is applied to branch b, there will be an additional negative sign between the two branches of the combined state. It changes the interference when it recombines. If the same negative sign is added to both, it is still only the overall phase and cannot change the interference.

sections.title: Back to crystal class
paragraphs: For a crystal’s finite subgroup of proper rotations, take its preimage in SU(2) and retain the central element representing a 2π rotation. This introduces double-valued representations and double groups. Point groups containing inversion or mirrors additionally need representations of those operations; SU(2)→SO(3) alone does not cover them.

Time reversal in a magnetic group acts antiunitarily on quantum states and includes complex conjugation; it is not an ordinary SU(2) unitary matrix. The three-dimensional picture of magnetic-moment reversal, the central minus sign of a spinor, and time reversal are related but distinct concepts.

example.title: Let only one interference path undergo 2π rotation
steps: The initial state is (|a⟩+|b⟩)⊗ψ/√2, and the path and spin are initially not entanglement .
Only on branch b, U(2π)=−I is used to obtain (|a⟩−|b⟩)⊗ψ/√2.
Define combined readout |+⟩=(|a⟩+|b⟩)/√2, |−⟩=(|a⟩−|b⟩)/√2.
The probability of the initial state being at the + port is 1; the probability of being at the − port after the action is 1. If both are multiplied together by −1, the reading is still at the + port.
example.result: What is observable is the relative phase between the two paths, and the overall negative sign of the isolated state cannot be regarded as a directly measurable quantity.

lessons.pitfall: "Returning to the original state after 4π" must mean returning to the same state vector; the measurement probability of a single pure state is already the same after 2π.

lessons.title: 06 · Representations: one group can act on different spaces
lessons.summary: Use three numbers 2, 3, and 8 to distinguish the group dimension, representation dimension and the spin label.
objectives: Explain why representations must preserve group multiplication
uses the 2j+1 rule of SU(2)
distinguishes between the three-dimensional representation of SU(2) and the basic representation of SU(3)

sections.title: A representation specifies what is transformed
paragraphs: A representation D maps every group element to a linear transformation of a vector space, satisfying D(g₁g₂)=D(g₁)D(g₂). One group can have many representations. Representation dimension counts components of the vectors acted upon and cannot be inferred from the group’s name alone.

A representation is reducible if a nonzero proper subspace is invariant under every D(g). Diagonalizing one generator alone does not decompose the representation; one must find subspaces invariant under all group operations simultaneously.

D(g₁g₂)=D(g₁)D(g₂)

sections.title: SU(2)
paragraphs: The finite-dimensional complex irreducible representation is labeled by j=0,1/2,1,3/2,… and has dimension 2j+1. j=1/2 is a two-component spinor; j=1 has three components and can be related to the rotation of a usual three-dimensional vector.

The central element −I acts in spin j as (−1)^(2j). For integer j this is +I, allowing the representation to descend to an ordinary SO(3) representation. For half-integer j, the two elements ±U cannot be identified.

sections.title: The 3 and 8 representations of SU(3)
paragraphs: The SU(3) fundamental representation acts on three-component complex vectors and has dimension 3; the group has eight independent real generators. Its adjoint representation acts on the Lie algebra by conjugation and has dimension 8.

The three-dimensional SU(2) representation and three-dimensional SU(3) fundamental representation have the same component count, but their acting groups and numbers of generators differ. SU(3) is not SO(3) or a more complete version of 3D crystal rotations. SU(3) can describe some ideal three-level controls; an actual material symmetry still requires a Hamiltonian check.

example.title: uses one 2π rotation to distinguish between the two SU(2) representations
steps: selects the same group of elements g=−I, which corresponds to a positive 2π rotation in space.
In j=1/2 representation, D(g)=(−1)¹I₂=−I₂.
In j=1 representation, D(g)=(−1)²I₃=+I₃.

The vector representation therefore maps the central element to the identity, while the two-component spinor representation retains the distinction. The vector representation is not a faithful representation of SU(2).
example.result: indicates how the group elements are perceived by the object; the same group does not guarantee the same representation matrix .

lessons.pitfall: "Three-dimensional representation" does not automatically equal three-dimensional real spatial rotation ; the group, real/complex vector space and specific functions must also be noted.

quiz.explanation: 2j+1=2×(3/2)+1=4; it is still the representation of SU(2) and will not become SU(4) just because of the four dimensions.

lessons.title: 07 · SU(3): Eight Gell-Mann generator
lessons.summary: Count eight directions in traceless Hermitian 3×3 matrices, then observe how three basis states mix.
objectives: Explain the origin of 3²−1=8
Recognize the Gell-Mann matrix and its normalization
Distinguish three-level mixing from physics spatial rotation

sections.title: Why exactly eight?
paragraphs: The three diagonal elements of the 3×3 Hermitian matrix are real numbers, and the three upper triangular non-diagonal elements each have a real part and an imaginary part, with a total of 3+2×3=9 real parameters. Then ask the trace to be zero, one less parameter, leaving 8. This is the dimension of su(3), which is the real dimension of SU(3).
Choose standard Gell-Mann matrices λ₁…λ₈ and Tₐ=λₐ/2, satisfying Tr(TₐTᵦ)=δₐᵦ/2. Rows and columns correspond to basis states |1⟩,|2⟩,|3⟩, not the spatial axes x,y,z.

sections.title: Embedded SU(2) vs. Complete SU(3)
paragraphs: The upper left 2×2 sub-blocks of λ₁, λ₂, and λ₃ are Pauli matrices, so they only mix |1⟩ and |2⟩, leaving |3⟩ unchanged. This subgroup is SU(2) embedded within SU(3) and does not yet cover all eight directions.

λ₄ and λ₅ connect |1⟩ and |3⟩; λ₆ and λ₇ connect |2⟩ and |3⟩. λ₃, λ₈ are diagonal matrices that change the phase without changing the probability in the selected basis. Looking only at probability histograms may miss phase changes, so read the complex amplitudes as well.

sections.title: Parameter period depends on generator
paragraphs: Do not apply the 4π period mechanism of SU(2) to each SU(3) generator . For T₁, the exponential period in the basic representation is 4π; for T₈=diag(1,1,−2)/(2√3), the minimum positive period is 4π√3. Real linear combinations of multiple generator define another single-parameter evolution whose period may be different or where there may be no finite positive period.
This experiment illustrates finite-dimensional matrices and transformations of ideal three-level states. It does not calculate quark dynamics or prove SU(3) symmetry in a crystal.

example.title: T₁ How to convert |1⟩ to |2⟩?
steps: The initial state is ψ₀=(1,0,0)ᵀ, and U₁(θ)=exp(−iθλ₁/2) is selected.
Use the SU(2) exponential formula within the first two components; the third component is a spectator: ψ(θ)=(cos(θ/2),−i sin(θ/2),0)ᵀ.
At θ=π, ψ(π)=(0,−i,0)ᵀ and the probabilities are (0,1,0).
At θ=2π, U₁=diag(−1,−1,1), which is not −I₃. The full matrix returns to I₃ only at θ=4π.
example.result: T₁ mixes a two-level subspace; the third component makes the global structure of SU(3) different from SU(2).

lessons.pitfall: Eight generators do not mean eight state amplitudes; the fundamental representation in this experiment always has only three complex components.

quiz.question: How many independent real parameters remain in a 3×3 Hermitian matrix after imposing zero trace?
quiz.explanation: Three real diagonal entries plus three complex off-diagonal entries give 9 real parameters. The traceless condition removes one, leaving 8.

quiz.question: U₁(θ)=exp(−iθλ₁/2) acts on |1⟩. What is the probability of measuring |2⟩ at θ=π?
quiz.explanation: The final state is −i|2⟩. The phase −i does not change the measurement probability of this basis state, so the probability is 1.

lessons.title: 08 · Cartan, weights, and roots: understanding SU(3)  weight diagram
lessons.summary: Use two simultaneously measurable generators to assign coordinates to three basis states, then obtain the six roots from differences of weights.
objectives: Read the three weights from the diagonal entries of T₃ and T₈
Distinguish fundamental-representation weights from the roots of  Lie algebra
Understand why weight-diagram coordinates are not atomic positions

sections.title: Two generators that can be diagonalized simultaneously
paragraphs: T₃ and T₈ commute and form a Cartan  generator ; SU(3) has rank 2. The two eigenvalues of a simultaneous eigenstate under these  generator  form a weight.

In the fundamental representation, the diagonal entries directly give the three weights w₁, w₂ and w₃, which form a triangle in the abstract (T₃,T₈) plane. A superposition is generally not a simultaneous eigenstate; its two expectation values are probability-weighted averages of the weights. This average point is not a new weight.

sections.title: Roots describe how generators connect different weights
paragraphs: Take i≠j and let Eᵢⱼ have its only nonzero entry, 1, in row i and column j. It maps |j⟩ to |i⟩. In the complexified  Lie algebra , [H,Eᵢⱼ]=(wᵢ(H)−wⱼ(H))Eᵢⱼ, so Eᵢⱼ corresponds to root αᵢⱼ=wᵢ−wⱼ. Eᵢⱼ need not itself be a  Hermitian  matrix; physical  Hermitian   generator  are combinations of it and Eⱼᵢ.

Pairwise differences of the three weights give six nonzero roots in opposite pairs. The adjoint representation also has two zero-weight directions corresponding to the Cartan subalgebra, hence dimension 6+2=8. Zero is not a root, and the three fundamental weights cannot simply be identified with the six roots.
sections.formula:

α₁₃=(1/2,√3/2)

sections.title: A j tag gives a irreducible representation
paragraphs: Finite-dimensional irreducible unitary representations of SU(2) are labeled by j=0,1/2,1,… and have dimension 2j+1. Using dimensionless angular momentum j⃗, physical angular momentum is ℏj⃗. In the |j,m⟩ basis, m increases from −j to j in steps of 1.

The total squared angular momentum j⃗² and jz can be diagonalized simultaneously. j⃗² has the fixed value j(j+1), independent of m; raising and lowering operators connect neighboring m values within the same irreducible representation.

sections.title: Why can the product space be rewritten as  direct sum ?
paragraphs: The state space of two combined systems is Vj₁⊗Vj₂, whose dimensions multiply. Under the same spatial rotation g, the group acts as Dj₁(g)⊗Dj₂(g): the tensor product of representations, also called their direct product. A basis change separates it into nonmixing total-angular-momentum subspaces, giving a direct sum ⊕ of irreducible representations.

If the two systems can rotate independently, the group is SU(2)×SU(2). Addition of angular momenta concerns common rotations, the diagonal SU(2) subgroup. Do not identify ×, ⊗, and ⊕ as the same operation.
sections.formula:
Vj₁⊗Vj₂ ≅ ⊕(J=|j₁−j₂|,…,j₁+j₂) VJ
J increases in steps of 1; each occurs once

sections.title: Basis-transformation amplitudes and physical measurements
paragraphs: The product basis |j₁,m₁⟩|j₂,m₂⟩ specifies the individual z components, while the coupled basis |J,M⟩ specifies total angular momentum. Only components with M=m₁+m₂ can occur. Clebsch–Gordan (CG) coefficients are the transformation amplitudes between these orthonormal bases; their squared moduli give measurement probabilities.

For example, combining atomic orbital l=1 with electron spin s=1/2 gives j=3/2 and j=1/2, containing 4+2=6 states in total. This decomposition groups the spin–orbit-split states; their actual energies also require an interaction Hamiltonian.

The triangle rule gives a minimum J of |1−1/2|=1/2 and a maximum of 3/2.
J changes in steps of 1, so only J=1/2 and J=3/2 occur.
The two subspaces contain 2 and 4 M values, respectively; their dimensions sum to 6.
example.result: 3⊗2=4⊕2; representation dimensions are conserved, and the group itself remains the same SU(2).

lessons.pitfall: Signs of CG coefficients depend on the basis-phase convention; align conventions before comparing tables. Probabilities, orthogonality, and total dimension are independent of an overall phase.

sections.title: How to regroup the four product states?
paragraphs: Order the product basis |↑↑⟩,|↑↓⟩,|↓↑⟩,|↓↓⟩. The maximal-M=1 state |↑↑⟩ must have J=1. Applying the total lowering operator gives the symmetric M=0 combination; lowering again gives |↓↓⟩, completing the triplet.

The remaining orthogonal combination is the J=0 singlet. It is invariant under common rotations U⊗U, while the three triplet components mix. Under this course’s phase convention, the |↑↓⟩ singlet coefficient is positive.

sections.title: Exchange action requires only total angular momentum label
paragraphs: Define dimensionless s⃗₁,s⃗₂ and H=κ s⃗₁·s⃗₂, with energy-unit κ. Reserve J for total-angular-momentum quantum number to avoid confusing it with exchange constants. From J⃗=s⃗₁+s⃗₂, expanding the square gives every J-subspace energy without evaluating a fourth-order determinant.

For κ>0 the singlet is lower, defining antiferromagnetic exchange under this sign convention; for κ<0 the triplet is lower. Ideal isotropic exchange preserves degeneracy of the three triplet components; fields or anisotropy can change this.

sections.title: From ideal dimer to observable quantity
paragraphs: This two-spin model is the starting point for understanding local magnetic moment dimers and exchange-coupled qubits. Interactive experiments can compare the sign of κ, CG amplitudes, and individual J multiplet energies, but do not automatically determine κ from the material structure.

Each singlet spin measured separately has no definite direction, yet the spins are correlated; they are not two fixed antiparallel classical arrows. Indistinguishable electrons must combine spatial, spin and other degrees of freedom into a fully antisymmetric wavefunction. Spin alone cannot determine whether the complete state is allowed.

sections.title: SU(3) requires two labels
paragraphs: SU(3) Rank 2, finite dimension irreducible representation Label highest weight with nonnegative integers (p,q). 3 corresponds to (1,0), the conjugate representation 3̄ corresponds to (0,1), and 8 corresponds to (1,1). Conjugation exchanges (p,q) for (q,p); two representation dimension are the same but not necessarily equivalent.

uses the (T3, T8) coordinates and simple positive roots w₁−w₂ and w₂−w₃ from the previous course. highest weight is pω₁+qω₂, among which ω₁=(1/2,1/(2√3)) and ω₂=(0,1/√3). The experimental weight diagram can show the same coordinate appearing multiple times; these are different states sharing a set of Cartan eigenvalues.

sections.title: dimension formula is not the same number as Casimir
paragraphs: Dimension represents the number of independent states in the space. The quadratic Casimir operator C₂=ΣₐTₐ² is commutated with all generator and is equivalent to a number multiplied by the identity matrix on irreducible representation . The formula relies on the normalization of generator ; Tr(TₐTᵦ)=δₐᵦ/2 in the basic representation is used here.

For (1,0), d=3 and C₂=4/3; for (1,1), d=8 and C₂=3. C₂ is dimensionless group-theory data, not automatically energy. The representations 3 and 3̄ have equal C₂, so the quadratic Casimir alone cannot distinguish all representations.

sections.title: Add weights first, then decompose
paragraphs: In a tensor product, a Cartan operator acts as T⊗I+I⊗T, so factor weights add. If multiple states share coordinates, add their multiplicities. Successively remove complete irreducible weight systems generated by highest weights to obtain the direct-sum decomposition. The plot’s outer outline alone misses internal states.

Note two kinds of multiplicity : 8 represents its own zero-weight multiplicity as 2; in the decomposition of 8⊗8, the entire 8 representation also appears twice. These two "2"s refer to different levels. The "Representation, Weights and tensor-product decomposition " experiment retains these two types of counts; for state-wise amplitudes please enter the new " Clebsch–Gordan coefficients and change of basis " experiments.

example.title: Why do (2,1) and (1,2) both have 15 states?
steps: Substitute (p,q)=(2,1) into the dimension formula to get d=3×2×5/2=15.
into Casimir's formula, we get C₂=(4+1+2+6+3)/3=16/3.
Exchanging the labels gives conjugate (1,2). Both formulas are invariant, so the dimension and C₂ remain unchanged.
But the orientation of highest weight and weight diagram changes; the same dimension and quadratic Casimir cannot prove that the two complex representation are equivalent.
example.result: (2,1) and (1,2) are a pair of conjugate 15-dimensional representations, and the necessary labels cannot be omitted just by "15".

sections.title: Two SU(3) symmetries, two different sets of indices
paragraphs: flavor SU(3) Approximate the light quark u, d, s as three components multiplet . It is an approximate global symmetry of the strong interaction: the difference in quark mass breaks it, and electromagnetic effects and so on cause additional differences, so the same multiplet does not have to be exactly the same mass.

Color SU(3) is QCD’s local gauge structure; its three components are color indices, not three flavors. Every flavor carries color, and flavor-dependent quark masses preserve color gauge invariance. Color-singlet and flavor-singlet conditions differ; gauge redundancy is not an ordinary observable spatial rotation.

sections.title: meson: a quark and an antiquark
paragraphs: At the group-theory level, the nine-dimensional space 3⊗3̄ can be viewed as matrices M. The common transformation M→UMU† leaves the trace part invariant, forming 1; the traceless part has eight dimensions and forms 8.

For flavor indices, this explains the grouping of light-meson multiplets; physical neutral mesons may also mix. For color indices, the usual quark–antiquark color singlet is (|r r̄⟩+|g ḡ⟩+|b b̄⟩)/√3. Color-octet components are not ordinary mesons that can be observed in isolation.

sections.title: Baryons: why are there two octets?
paragraphs: First combine two 3 representations: symmetric tensors give 6 and antisymmetric tensors give 3̄. Combining with the third 3 gives 6⊗3=10⊕8 and 3̄⊗3=8⊕1, so the two different coupling channels each contribute one octet.

Color indices can be contracted into a singlet with the fully antisymmetric ε_{abc}. The flavor-space 10,8,8,1 components must also be combined with spin, orbitals, and fermionic statistics. The decomposition itself neither assigns an equally light particle to every term nor calculates masses or lifetimes.

example.title: Find the group-theoretic meson singlet through trace decomposition
steps: Identify the nine basis states |i⟩|j̄⟩ with matrix units Eij.
The diagonal combination E11+E22+E33=I is unchanged under M→UMU†.
Normalization gives |1⟩=(|1 1̄⟩+|2 2̄⟩+|3 3̄⟩)/√3.
The orthogonal space of traceless matrices has dimension 9−1=8 and forms the adjoint octet.
example.result: The singlet comes from an invariant index contraction. Flavor and color interpretations of those indices have different physical meanings.

lessons.pitfall: 3⊗3=6⊕3̄ contains no singlet; conjugate representations must be retained when distinguishing quark–quark from quark–antiquark products. Approximate flavor symmetry does not mean that quark masses break color gauge symmetry.

sections.title: The same irreducible representation can occur more than once
paragraphs: In an SU(2) tensor product of two irreducible representations, each allowed J occurs once. SU(3) does not share this general property: 8⊗8 contains two equivalent 8 representations in independent subspaces. They cannot be combined into one 16-dimensional irreducible representation.

For two identical octet factors, one can additionally study the exchange operator. The symmetric part has dimension 8×9/2=36 and splits into 27, 8s, and 1; the antisymmetric part has dimension 8×7/2=28 and splits into 10, 10̄, and 8a. The labels s and a refer to exchange of the two factors, rather than new SU(3)  highest weight .

sections.title: Allowed by group theory does not mean dynamically realized
paragraphs: For an operator transforming as R_{op}, a matrix element from R_i to R_f can be nonzero only if R_f occurs in R_{op}⊗R_i. Its multiplicity counts independent reduced channels; the actual amplitude also depends on dynamics, other conservation laws, and the states' quantum numbers.

For example, an octet operator acting on an octet initial state in the SU(3) symmetric limit has two octet channels, distinguished by an extra index. Their existence determines neither their coupling constants nor whether both are nonzero. For identical particles, spatial, spin, and other components must jointly satisfy total exchange symmetry; antisymmetric internal states cannot all be discarded indiscriminately.

sections.title: Make three cross-checks in the interactive experiment
paragraphs: Choose two representations and check that the product dimension equals the sum of irreducible dimensions times their multiplicities. Then check weight-by-weight multiplicities in the diagrams, and finally whether the physical problem actually has the assumed SU(3) symmetry.

The “Representations, weights, and  tensor-product decomposition ” experiment calculates  highest weight ,  multiplicity , dimensions, and Casimirs, and displays weight counting. The “ Clebsch–Gordan coefficients  and  change of basis ” experiment additionally constructs state-resolved bases, offers numerical and exact-radical modes, and identifies exchange-symmetric 8s and 8a for 8⊗8. Neither experiment predicts scattering cross sections or decay rates.

example.title: Can an octet operator take a singlet into an octet?
steps: The initial representation is R_i=1, and the operator transforms as R_{op}=8.
Calculate 8⊗1=8 to obtain the unique octet channel.
Thus the final representation R_f=8 is not forbidden by this SU(3) selection rule, while R_f=1 does not appear in the decomposition.
Other quantum numbers and reduced matrix elements must still be checked. Not forbidden does not imply a nonzero probability.
example.result: Representation decomposition selects possible channels; actual transition strengths require a separate calculation.

lessons.pitfall: Dimensions summing to 64 are only a necessary check; dimensions alone do not determine the decomposition. Nor does the multiplicity of the two 8 representations mean that their two sets of CG coefficients have already been calculated.

sections.title: One state, two coordinate systems
paragraphs: Write the orthonormal product basis as |i,j⟩ and the coupled basis as |R,α,μ⟩. R=(p,q) specifies  irreducible representation , α distinguishes copies of the same R, and μ labels basis states within that representation. The  Clebsch–Gordan coefficients  C_(ij),(Rαμ)=⟨i,j|R,α,μ⟩ are the amplitudes of coupled states in the product basis. Each column of C is an entire coupled basis vector, not a probability table.

If product-basis coordinates are a and coupled-basis coordinates are b, then a=Cb and b=C†a. The basis changes, but the physical state does not. For a normalized state, squared coordinate magnitudes give the probabilities of the corresponding basis states. Even when the CG matrix used here is real, the input state may have complex amplitudes; † must be retained in the general basis-transformation formula.

sections.title: Why is checking the dimension alone insufficient?
paragraphs: Any square matrix with orthonormal columns passes the C†C=I check, but may fail to split the SU(3) action into the correct irreducible blocks. The product-space  generator  is Gₐ=Tₐ⁽¹⁾⊗I+I⊗Tₐ⁽²⁾. A genuine CG matrix must also transform every  generator  into the corresponding representation blocks.

The experiment labels basis states by GT patterns and provides matrices, expansion terms, channel probabilities and validation results. Small numerical residuals indicate that floating-point calculations satisfy the equalities to the current precision; exact mode also retains simplifiable algebraic expressions. Checking only the quadratic Casimir does not uniquely determine the basis transformation: 10 and 10̄, for example, have the same quadratic Casimir but are different representations.

Gₐ C=C Dₐ，Dₐ=⊕R,α Tₐ⁽R⁾
P(R,α)=Σμ |bRαμ|²
P(R)=Σα P(R,α)

sections.title: Compare phases together with basis labels
paragraphs: Changing the overall phase of a coupled basis vector changes its CG column without changing the physical direction spanned by that column. The corresponding coordinate b must change by the opposite phase to keep a=Cb invariant. Comparing the sign of a single tabulated coefficient cannot establish a conflict between conventions.

The input representations use orthonormal GT bases, with positive nonzero coefficients for adjacent raising operators. The fundamental basis is ordered u, d, s; the antifundamental basis corresponds to s̄, −d̄, ū. Here u, d and s are initially just names for three abstract basis states; flavor or color interpretations require a separate statement. The first nonzero product-basis coordinate of a highest-weight vector is chosen positive, and the remaining states in that representation are constructed using the fixed generator convention.

example.title: Transform a two-state superposition with a relative phase into symmetric and antisymmetric bases
steps: In the subspace 3⊗3 define S=(|u,d⟩+|d,u⟩)/√2 and A=(|u,d⟩−|d,u⟩)/√2. Write C=[[1,1],[1,−1]]/√2 using product-basis order (|u,d⟩,|d,u⟩) and coupled-basis order (S, A).
Take a=(1,i)ᵀ/√2, so the two product amplitudes differ in phase by π/2. Then b=C†a gives b=((1+i)/2,(1−i)/2)ᵀ.
Both coupled-channel probabilities are 1/2. These are squared moduli of complex amplitudes; directly squaring an amplitude or retaining only its real part gives incorrect results.
Calculate Cb next. Its first entry is 1/√2 and its second is i/√2, recovering the original product coordinates.
example.result: A round-trip basis transformation restores all complex amplitudes. Probabilities sum to 1, but probabilities alone cannot replace amplitudes in the inverse transformation.

lessons.pitfall: The columns of C expand coupled basis vectors in the product basis, so the product-to-coupled transformation uses C†. Do not infer the matrix-multiplication direction from an arrow label alone.

lessons.title: 16 · construct CG states for 3⊗3 and 3⊗3̄
lessons.summary: Start from exchange symmetry and trace decomposition to obtain normalized amplitudes that can be checked term by term.
objectives: Construct symmetric and antisymmetric states in 6 and 3̄
Convert the natural antifundamental basis into the experiment's GT basis
Distinguish total octet probability from the choice of basis within the octet

sections.title: Two 3 representations: exchange splits the nine-dimensional space into 6+3
paragraphs: The exchange operator P₁₂ maps |i,j⟩ to |j,i⟩. For equal factor representations, it commutes with the diagonal SU(3) action. The three |i,i⟩ states and three normalized symmetric combinations form a six-dimensional space; three normalized antisymmetric combinations form a three-dimensional space, giving 3⊗3=6⊕3̄.

For example, a single product state |u,d⟩ generally does not belong to a definite irreducible channel. It is an equal-weight superposition of symmetric S and antisymmetric A, so the probabilities of 6 and 3̄ are both 1/2. The symmetry signs describe exchange of the two factors, not directly whether they are physical bosons or fermions.

sections.title: 3 and 3̄: the identity-matrix direction is the singlet
paragraphs: Start from the natural conjugate basis (ū,d̄,s̄), identifying |i,j̄⟩ with matrix units Eij. The action is M→UMU†, so the identity-matrix direction is invariant. The normalized singlet is (|u,ū⟩+|d,d̄⟩+|s,s̄⟩)/√3; traceless matrices orthogonal to it form the octet.

In this natural basis, choose two orthogonal zero-weight octet states D=(|u,ū⟩−|d,d̄⟩)/√2 and H=(|u,ū⟩+|d,d̄⟩−2|s,s̄⟩)/√6. Together with the six off-diagonal matrix units, they form an orthonormal octet basis. Other consistent basis phases or choices within an equal-weight subspace are also valid.

sections.title: Why can the program's singlet contain a minus sign?
paragraphs: The experiment labels the GT basis of 3 as (g₀,g₁,g₂)=(u,d,s) and that of 3̄ as (h₀,h₁,h₂)=(s̄,−d̄,ū). Thus the same physical singlet has program coordinates (|g₀,h₂⟩−|g₁,h₁⟩+|g₂,h₀⟩)/√3. The middle minus sign cancels the minus in the definition of h₁ and does not break SU(3) invariance.

When comparing analytic expressions, first check representation labels, GT patterns, row order, and phases. In this program's  highest weight   phase convention , the two zero-weight octet states are D and −H above. Thus the program amplitude of |u,ū⟩ in the second octet state is −1/√6, while the probability remains 1/6. The experiment provides the actual full-column expansion; using it directly for the inverse transformation is the most reliable approach. For color indices, this singlet is the color-invariant quark–antiquark combination; the singlet of flavor SU(3) belongs to a different physical classification.

example.title: Why is the singlet projection 1/3 rather than 1?
steps: Take |u,ū⟩ as the initial state, a normalized basis vector in the nine-dimensional product space.
Taking the inner product with the normalized singlet gives ⟨1|u,ū⟩=1/√3, hence singlet probability 1/3.
Subtracting the singlet projection leaves |u,ū⟩−(|u,ū⟩+|d,d̄⟩+|s,s̄⟩)/3, a traceless octet vector with squared norm 2/3.
In the natural zero-weight basis D,H, the octet coordinates are 1/√2,1/√6; their squared moduli still sum to 2/3.
example.result: “Matching indices in the initial state” does not make it a singlet. A SU(3) singlet requires a coherent superposition of three natural diagonal product states with specified phases.

lessons.pitfall: 3̄ is not simply 3 with renamed states. The conjugate generators, basis order and phases must all be transformed consistently; a positive-coefficient singlet in the natural basis may have a minus sign in GT coordinates.

lessons.title: 17 · Two octets:  outer multiplicity , exchange, and conventions
lessons.summary: The same (p,q) can occur more than once. A complete CG matrix must also specify how bases are chosen among these copies.
objectives: Distinguish weight multiplicity from outer multiplicity of an irreducible representation
Use the exchange operator to label 8s and 8a in 8⊗8
Identify probabilities that depend on the outer-multiplicity basis and totals that remain invariant

sections.title: Multiplicities at two different levels
paragraphs: 8⊗8=27⊕10⊕10̄⊕8⊕8⊕1. Here “8 occurs twice” means  outer multiplicity  2; α=1,2 distinguishes the two eight-dimensional copies. Each 8 also has two zero-weight basis states, giving weight  multiplicity  2, which requires internal state labels. Specifying only (p, q) and the two Cartan eigenvalues therefore does not always identify a column uniquely.

Two equivalent octets form a sixteen-dimensional isotypic subspace, written ℂ²⊗V₈. SU(3) acts as the identity on the first factor. Specifying the SU(3) representation alone therefore still allows an arbitrary unitary basis change in this two-dimensional copy space; a CG table needs an additional outer-multiplicity convention.

sections.title: Exchange symmetry provides meaningful copy labels
paragraphs: For identical factors, this experiment also resolves the exchange operator P₁₂. For 8⊗8, it selects the two octets as 8s with P₁₂=+1 and 8a with P₁₂=−1. The copy label then carries exchange information rather than merely a number. The  highest weight  phase and remaining orthogonalization order must still be fixed to make every coefficient reproducible.

The symmetric and antisymmetric sectors have dimensions 36 and 28. Exchange labels refer to exchange of tensor factors, without automatically incorporating a particle's spin, orbitals or statistics. All degrees of freedom must be combined to decide whether a total physical-particle state is allowed.

sections.title: Changing the copy basis is not a physical transition
paragraphs: Let the amplitudes of two copies with the same internal label μ be b=(bs,ba). If the copy basis is multiplied by a unitary matrix R, the new coordinates are b′=R†b. Individual copy probabilities may change, but their sum and the projection onto the entire octet isotypic subspace remain invariant. If basis states must also have definite exchange eigenvalues, 8s and 8a can no longer be mixed arbitrarily.

Physical interactions require reduced matrix elements or coupling constants. A complete CG table relates group-theoretic state labels to amplitudes, but cannot alone predict decay rates or spectra. Two outer-multiplicity channels may carry independent dynamical parameters; their amplitudes must not be merged merely because both have label (1,1).

b′=R†b
|bs′|²+|ba′|²=|bs|²+|ba|²

example.title: Rotate a pair of copy basis vectors by 45°
steps: For the same internal label μ, use |s⟩=|8s,μ⟩ and |a⟩=|8a,μ⟩ as the original basis. Choose initial state |s⟩, with coordinates (1,0).
Define |+⟩=(|s⟩+|a⟩)/√2 and |−⟩=(−|s⟩+|a⟩)/√2. This is a unitary  change of basis  in copy space.
Inner products give new coordinates (1/√2,−1/√2), each with probability 1/2; their total is still 1.
In the new basis, the original exchange operator is [[0,−1],[−1,0]]. The new basis vectors no longer have definite exchange eigenvalues, but the initial state's exchange expectation remains +1.
example.result: Individual-copy probabilities depend on the chosen copy basis. Complete projections and physical operator expectations remain invariant after consistent  change of basis .

lessons.pitfall: 8s and 8a are not new SU(3) irreducible types. Mixing their state coordinates without also transforming the exchange-operator matrix creates an artificial inconsistency.

lessons.title: 18 · Higher-dimensional representations: 10⊗3 and 27⊗3
lessons.summary: Start from Dynkin labels and the rule for adding one box: determine the channels first, then examine the full state-resolved CG matrix.
objectives: Use (p,q) to distinguish equal-dimensional but inequivalent representations
Derive the  tensor product  decomposition of arbitrary (p, q) with the fundamental representation 3
Distinguish the input-label limit, product-space dimension and output-representation labels

sections.title: Two representations of dimension fifteen need not be the same representation
paragraphs: A SU(3)  irreducible representation  is specified by nonnegative integers (p, q). 10=(3,0) and 27=(2,2) have dimensions 10 and 27. Both (4,0) and (2,1) have dimension 15 but different  highest weight . Although (4,0) is often denoted 15′, a dimension alone is insufficient. The experiment always displays both dimension and Dynkin labels.

The conjugate representation has labels (q,p). For example, 10̄=(0,3), while (1,3) and (3,1) are conjugates, both of dimension 24. Shorthand names 24 and 24̄ vary between references; below we write 24_(1,3) explicitly rather than infer conjugacy from the shorthand alone.

sections.title: Coupling to 3: three allowed box-addition positions
paragraphs: Write (p, q) as Young-diagram row lengths (p+q, q,0). Coupling to the fundamental 3 adds one box. Adding it to the first row gives (p+1, q); the second row requires p≥1 and gives (p−1, q+1); the third row requires q≥1 and, after removing a complete column of three boxes, gives (p, q−1). Terms with negative labels must be omitted.

Thus 10⊗3 has two channels, with dimensions 15+15=30; 27⊗3 has three channels, with dimensions 42+24+15=81. Every channel here has outer multiplicity 1. The decomposition fixes subspace types, while the complete CG matrix further determines the expansion of each coupled basis state.

sections.title: Even high-dimensional matrices begin with small equal-weight subspaces
paragraphs: CG coefficients connect only product and coupled states of the same total weight. Even for an 81-row matrix, first inspect a chosen coupled column or product row, checking its nonzero entries and GT patterns, then view the full matrix. Zero coefficients are not missing data: they follow from weight conservation or orthogonality.

Numerical mode allows p+q≤4 for each input factor and product dimension N≤256. Exact mode uses the same input-label bound with N limited to 81. These are resource limits for interactive calculation. Output representations are not restricted by the input label-sum bound; for example, (3,2), with p+q=5, can occur in 27⊗3.

example.title: Check each channel of 27⊗3 against the total dimension 81
steps: The 27 has label (2,2), corresponding to Young-diagram row lengths (4,2,0). All three allowed positions for adding one box are available.
The three row-length sets are (5,2,0), (4,3,0), and (4,2,1). Removing a complete three-box column from the third gives (3,1,0).
Converting back gives Dynkin labels (3,2), (1,3), and (2,1), with dimensions 4×3×7/2=42, 2×4×6/2=24, and 3×2×5/2=15.
Their dimensions sum to 81=27×3. Select a column in the experiment to see how a definite GT state expands over 81 product coordinates; a dimension check alone cannot replace these coefficients.
example.result: 27⊗3=(3,2)⊕(1,3)⊕(2,1), with dimension check 42+24+15=81; each type occurs once.

lessons.pitfall: 15′=(4,0) and 15=(2,1) have equal dimensions but are inequivalent. The representation dimension, product-space dimension N, and group dimension 8 are three different concepts.

lessons.title: 19 · from integer weights to exact radical CG coefficients
lessons.summary: Retain rational numbers and radicals throughout the construction, turning a small numerical residual into a simplifiable algebraic equality.
objectives: Distinguish symbolic construction, floating-point calculation and guessing radicals from decimals
Obtain a higher-dimensional CG block by lowering a highest-weight state
Verify exact normalization, orthogonality, and  intertwining relation

sections.title: What does exact mean?
paragraphs: Numerical mode uses double-precision floating-point arithmetic for larger matrices and rapid inspection. Exact mode starts from integer GT patterns, rational numbers, and positive square roots, solving equations and normalizing algebraically. A displayed sqrt(3)/2 is constructed exactly, rather than guessed from 0.866025… as a nearby radical.

For example, 1/3 is an exact rational number, whereas the finite decimal 0.3333333333 is a different number. To request exact results, specify inputs with explicit expressions such as 1/3 or sqrt(2)/2. Exact matrices also provide numerical approximations for heatmaps and amplitude comparisons; those approximations cannot replace the symbolic expressions.

sections.title: 10⊗3: √3/2 and 1/2 appear after a single lowering step
paragraphs: Let h be the highest-weight state of 10=(3,0), and l its normalized adjacent lowered state, with E₂₁h=√3 l. In the fundamental representation, E₂₁u=d. The product-space lowering operator is F=E₂₁⊗I+I⊗E₂₁, so F|h,u⟩=|h,d⟩+√3|l,u⟩. The two product states are orthogonal, and this vector has norm 2.

After normalization, this lowered state of 15′=(4,0) is v=(|h,d⟩+√3|l,u⟩)/2. The vector w=(√3|h,d⟩−|l,u⟩)/2, orthogonal to it at the same weight, is annihilated by both simple-root  raising operator  and becomes the  highest weight  state of 15=(2,1). Its first nonzero product coordinate is chosen positive, matching the experiment's convention.

sections.title: Radicals do not remove basis conventions
paragraphs: Exactness guarantees algebraic equalities for the specified algebra and conventions, not coefficient-by-coefficient sign agreement with another CG table. The GT order, factor order,  highest weight  phases, and choices of  outer multiplicity  copies must still be stated. When a weight has multiple states, the program coordinates them through the complete  generator  relations; column signs cannot be changed independently at will.

For 8⊗8, exchange eigenvalues distinguish 8s from 8a; more general outer-multiplicity spaces still require a definite orthogonalization rule. Checking only C†C=I does not establish that the channels are correct; GₐC=CDₐ must also be checked. The experiment retains exact expressions, conventions and validation information for term-by-term reproduction.

example.title: Transform the product state |h,d⟩ into the two fifteen-dimensional channels
steps: With product-basis order (x, y) and coupled-basis order (v, w), place the expansion coefficients in columns to obtain C=[[1/2,√3/2],[√3/2,−1/2]].
The first column has norm 1/4+3/4=1, as does the second; their inner product is √3/4−√3/4=0.
The initial state x has product coordinates a=(1,0)ᵀ; b=C†a=(1/2,√3/2)ᵀ.
The two channel probabilities are 1/4 and 3/4. Calculating Cb=(1,0)ᵀ then cancels the second coordinate exactly.
example.result: This initial state has probability 1/4 in the 15′ channel and 3/4 in the (2,1) channel. The exact radicals also retain relative signs needed for the reverse basis transformation.

lessons.pitfall: Guessing a radical from a decimal with a dozen digits is not proof of an exact construction. Exact mode also limits input dimensions and expression lengths; it does not claim support for arbitrary-dimensional SU(3) inputs.

lessons.title: 20 · Exact complex amplitudes: basis changes, interference and round-trip checks
lessons.summary: A CG matrix can contain real radicals while the state has imaginary components. Exact expressions help verify phases, norms, and inverse transformations.
objectives: Enter exact complex amplitudes with separate real and imaginary parts
Obtain normalized probabilities from amplitudes without losing phases
Use the exact output as inverse-transformation input and verify the original state

sections.title: Specify complex numbers explicitly to preserve coherence
paragraphs: In the two-dimensional subspace of 3⊗3, take x=|u,d⟩, y=|d,u⟩ and the exact state ψ=(x+i y)/√2. Enter real and imaginary parts separately: for example, x has amplitude {re:"sqrt(2)/2",im:"0"}, y has {re:"0",im:"sqrt(2)/2"}, and all other positions in the full vector are zero. The imaginary-part field represents i, so I need not be entered in a real-valued field.

Each input real or imaginary part permits restricted integers, rational numbers, arithmetic operations, and sqrt(nonnegative integer) expressions. Use the string 1/1000 for one thousandth, rather than 1e-3 or a decimal; JSON numbers are converted to rationals according to their decimal value. Reverse an exact state using its exact output expressions; copying truncated display decimals introduces a new approximation.

sections.title: Probabilities do not contain complete  change of basis  information
paragraphs: The S and A coordinates above both have probability 1/2, but their amplitudes are different complex numbers. Keeping only these probabilities and taking positive square roots produces a different state. The inverse transformation requires each amplitude's real part, imaginary part and relative sign.

For an unnormalized vector, the program retains the input scale and computes probabilities as |bₖ|²/Σⱼ|bⱼ|². The squared norm is the same before and after changing basis, but individual channel probabilities need not be. The inverse-transformation button uses the complete output vector, not the truncated nonzero-entry table.

sections.title: When  multiplicity  occurs, check labels before coefficients
paragraphs: Exact mode still records each column's irreducible type (p,q), copy label and GT pattern. Weight multiplicity within one representation and outer multiplicity of an entire representation are different indices. Omitting them can cause two exact radicals to be incorrectly compared as entries in the same column.

Changing basis gives new coordinates for the same state. If an operator A is also transformed, its new matrix is C†AC, preserving a†Aa=b†(C†AC)b. An exact basis transformation neither generates time evolution nor determines interaction coupling constants from group-theoretic channels.

A coupled =C†A product C
a†A product a=b†A coupled b

example.title: Complete an exact round trip using full complex amplitudes
steps: In the exact complex-phase preset, the initial state is (|u,d⟩+i|d,u⟩)/√2, with squared norm exactly 1.
Product→coupled gives S amplitude (1+i)/2 and A amplitude (1−i)/2; all remaining coupled coordinates vanish.
Both squared magnitudes are ((1)²+(1)²)/4=1/2. Use the two complete complex amplitudes as coupled inputs and switch to coupled→product.
The x coordinate is [(1+i)+(1−i)]/(2√2)=1/√2, and the y coordinate is [(1+i)−(1−i)]/(2√2)=i/√2. All complex coordinates are recovered.
example.result: An exact round trip recovers every complex amplitude and the norm. Matching probabilities is only one of these checks.

lessons.pitfall: A real CG matrix does not require real state amplitudes. Squared magnitudes lose phase and cannot replace a complex vector in the inverse transformation.

lessons.title: 21 · Triple  tensor product : from  coupling path  to a Racah matrix
lessons.summary: Fix the final representation first, then label every path by its intermediate representation and two outer multiplicities. Recoupling connects two bases of the same subspace.
objectives: Distinguish rebracketing, factor exchange, and time evolution
Calculate the  multiplicity  of the final representation through two  tensor product  decompositions
Derive F=V_R†V_L and the inverse transformation from two isometric embeddings

sections.title: Bracketing changes which intermediate channel is resolved first
paragraphs: For representations A, B, and C, first coupling A and B gives ((A⊗B)⊗C); first coupling B and C gives A⊗(B⊗C). Both retain factor order A, B, C. Changing brackets changes the intermediate representation used to classify states; it does not exchange A and C.

For fixed final irreducible representation D, write a left path as e=(E,α,β): E occurs in A⊗B, α distinguishes copies of E, and β distinguishes copies of D in E⊗C. A right path f=(F,γ,δ) similarly comes from B⊗C→F and A⊗F→D. E or F alone is insufficient when outer multiplicities occur.

e=(E,α: A⊗B→E, β: E⊗C→D)
f=(F,γ: B⊗C→F, δ: A⊗F→D)

sections.title: The Racah matrix acts in copy space
paragraphs: D occurs m_D times in the triple product; this  isotypic subspace  can be written ℂ^(m_D)⊗V_D. m_D counts copies and dim D counts internal states in each copy; their product is the  isotypic subspace  dimension. For one fixed internal GT state μ of D, each side has m_D path states. The Racah matrix acts between these path coordinates.

Expand left and right path states in the same A⊗B⊗C product basis and use them as columns of V_L and V_R. They are orthonormal and span the copy space of the same D and μ, so F=V_R†V_L is unitary. Here rows of F label right paths and columns label left paths: b=Fa transforms left coordinates a to right coordinates, and a=F†b transforms back.

F_fe=⟨f,D,μ|e,D,μ⟩
V_L=V_R F, F†F=FF†=I_(m_D)
b=Fa, a=F†b
The block in the triple space is F⊗I_(dim D)

sections.title: Why need F not be defined anew for every internal state?
paragraphs: The full embedding of every path intertwines the same SU(3) generators. By Schur's lemma, the operator between two embeddings is a scalar times the identity on the irreducible space V_D, so a path coefficient of F is independent of the internal GT state μ. Highest-weight states construct the minimal multiplicity space; consistently lowering the same embeddings gives the same recoupling matrix.

The interface selects the final D and path amplitudes, rather than an arbitrary N-dimensional state in the full triple product. Choose one left path to inspect its probability distribution over right paths, then reverse the complete output. If D is absent from the decomposition, no corresponding path space exists; choose a different final representation.

The triple  recoupling  experiment supports inputs 1, 3, 3̄, 6, 6̄, and 8, namely p+q≤2, with total product dimension at most 512. Exact mode constructs rationals and radicals directly and also provides a numerical preview. Any irreducible type actually present in the triple product may be selected as the final representation. These limits are stated separately from the input and matrix-dimension limits of the binary CG experiment.

example.title: Why does the final 3 occur twice in 3⊗3̄⊗3?
steps: First compute A⊗B=3⊗3̄=8⊕1. Both 8⊗3 and 1⊗3 contain one 3, giving left paths E=8,1.
On the other side, first compute B⊗C=3̄⊗3=8⊕1; 3⊗8 and 3⊗1 each contain one 3, yielding right paths F=8 and 1.
Each binary channel on either side has outer multiplicity 1, so m_3=2. The triple-product space has dimension 27, while the final-3 isotypic subspace has dimension 2×3=6.
For a fixed internal state of the final 3, the Racah matrix is 2×2. The experiment displays intermediate channels and copy indices and calculates the exact transformation between the two paths.
example.result: The Racah matrix size is determined by the path  multiplicity  of the final representation. Here it is 2×2, neither 3×3 nor 27×27.

lessons.pitfall: Associativity guarantees the same total space, not identical intermediate-channel bases term by term. Changing brackets is a basis change; exchanging factors additionally requires a specified permutation operator.

lessons.title: 22 · Exact Racah and 6j coefficients: radicals from three 3 representations
lessons.summary: Compute overlaps directly in the highest-weight subspace spanned by three product states, then distinguish the unitary Racah matrix from dimension-scaled 6j coefficients.
objectives: Construct both octet path bases from exchange symmetry and the  highest weight  condition
Obtain 1/2 and √3/2 from exact inner products, rather than guessing radicals from decimals
Interpret SU(3) 6j coefficients using explicit dimension normalization and outer-multiplicity labels

sections.title: Octet  highest weight  space of three fundamental representations
paragraphs: 3⊗3⊗3=10⊕8⊕8⊕1. For the final D=8=(1,1), left paths come from E=6,3̄ and right paths from F=6,3̄. Both paths have outer multiplicity 1. Let x=|u,u,d⟩, y=|u,d,u⟩ and z=|d,u,u⟩; they are orthonormal and share total weight (H₁,H₂)=(1,1).

The total raising operator E₁₂ maps x,y,z to |u,u,u⟩, so an octet highest-weight state requires its three coefficients to sum to zero; E₂₃ already annihilates these states. Symmetry or antisymmetry of the first two factors defines the left paths, and of the last two defines the right paths. The following phases match the experiment's GT convention.
sections.formula:
L₆=(2x−y−z)/√6, L₃̄=(y−z)/√2
R₆=(x+y−2z)/√6, R₃̄=(x−y)/√2
Left-path order (6,3̄); right-path order (6,3̄)

sections.title: Four inner products form an exact F matrix
paragraphs: For example, ⟨R₆|L₆⟩=(2−1+2)/6=1/2 and ⟨R₆|L₃̄⟩=(1+2)/√12=√3/2. The remaining overlaps are √3/2 and −1/2. Every coefficient is an overlap of exact orthonormal vectors, without reconstructing radicals from decimals.

Each column's squared moduli sum to 1, and distinct columns have zero inner product. Here F is real symmetric and happens to satisfy F†=F; this is not required of a general complex unitary  recoupling  matrix. Reordering paths or changing a complete path's phase correspondingly reorders or changes an entire row or column of F.

sections.title: The 6j normalization used here
paragraphs: Racah matrix elements are overlaps between unit-normalized bases. To provide a separate 6j table, this classroom defines S_fe=F_fe/√[dim(E_e) dim(F_f)], retaining all outer-multiplicity indices within e and f. This uses the ordinary-group q→1 form of the dimension normalization in the cited reference, while retaining this project's GT phases and path order.

The rescaled S is generally no longer  unitary matrix . If D_E and D_F are the diagonal matrices of left and right intermediate  representation dimension , then S†D_F S=D_E⁻¹. F still performs coordinate transformations; S must not directly multiply amplitudes. Standard SU(2) 6j formulas also contain their own  phase convention . One cannot merely replace j with SU(3) labels (p, q), or omit  outer multiplicity  indices.

example.title: Predict right-channel probabilities from the left 6 path
steps: Choose initial state L₆ with left-path amplitudes a=(1,0)ᵀ, fixing one internal state of the final 8.
Using b=Fa gives b=(1/2,√3/2)ᵀ, corresponding to right paths F=6 and 3̄.
The probabilities are 1/4 and 3/4, summing to 1. Applying F†b gives a=(1,0)ᵀ, with exact cancellation of cross terms.
The corresponding 6j entries are 1/12 and √6/12. These are overlaps divided by dimension factors; their squared moduli are not the channel probabilities in this experiment.
example.result: In this convention, L₆ has probabilities 1/4 and 3/4 in right paths 6 and 3̄. F performs  change of basis , while S provides an explicitly normalized 6j table.

lessons.title: 23 · Complex phases and two-body operators in  recoupling
lessons.summary: Track path-amplitude phases exactly, and move a two-factor interaction that is diagonal in one coupling basis into another.
objectives: Perform an exact round-trip recoupling of complex path amplitudes
Distinguish path probabilities, projection onto the complete final representation, and internal state labels
Express the right-hand two-body operator in left-path coordinates using F†O_R F

sections.title: A real F also carries complex phases
paragraphs: Choose left-path state ψ=(L₆+iL₃̄)/√2 in 3⊗3⊗3→8. CG and F may be real radicals in this experiment's convention, but state coordinates may still be complex. Exact input separates real and imaginary parts and accepts restricted expressions using integers, rationals, and sqrt(nonnegative integer). The reverse button transfers the complete exact output.

Multiplication by F gives b₆=(1+i√3)/(2√2) and b₃̄=(√3−i)/(2√2), each with probability exactly 1/2. These match the two left-coordinate probabilities but are not the same complex vector; comparing probabilities alone misses the phase change. For unnormalized vectors, the basis change preserves the amplitude scale, and reported probabilities are divided by the squared norm.

sections.title: Why do two-body operators require recoupling?
paragraphs: If a SU(3)-invariant operator acts only on B and C, it is often easier to express it in the right-path basis that couples B⊗C first. For O=κΣₐ Tₐ^(B)Tₐ^(C) and specified intermediate representation F, the eigenvalue is κ[C₂(F)−C₂(B)−C₂(C)]/2. Here κ is a separately specified model parameter; group theory does not determine its value.

For the same state, b=Fa, so the operator matrix in left-path coordinates is O_L=F†O_R F. Thus an interaction between one factor pair can be diagonal in its own channels yet mix multiple paths under different brackets. This is a model derivation on paper: the experiment supplies F and amplitudes for checking, rather than computing specific material or hadron dynamics.
sections.formula:
O=κΣₐ Tₐ^(B)Tₐ^(C)
ε_F=κ[C₂(F)−C₂(B)−C₂(C)]/2
O_L=F†O_R F
a†O_La=b†O_Rb

sections.title: Retain every level of labels as multiplicities increase
paragraphs: More generally, paths e=(E,α,β) and f=(F,γ,δ) may have  outer multiplicity  at either binary-coupling step. Every copy must occupy its own row or column. Path probabilities may be aggregated by intermediate representation, but exact inversion requires the full complex amplitude of every path. Internal GT equal-weight  multiplicity  within one final representation must not be merged with these path labels.

For example, 8⊗8⊗8→8 has path multiplicity 8: intermediate 27,10,10̄ and 1 each contribute one path; intermediate 8 has two copies, and each couples with the third 8 to the final 8 through two channels, contributing 2×2=4 paths. F is therefore 8×8. Exchange-copy labels at both vertices must be retained, not represented by a single 8s or 8a label.

Exact symbolic results satisfy equalities in the specified basis convention. Changing left and right copy bases by U_L,U_R gives F′=U_R†F U_L; state coordinates and operators must transform consistently. Entry-by-entry sign agreement between arbitrary tables is not a physical invariant. Compare complete norms, projections, and expectation values after consistent basis transformations.

example.title: Express the B–C interaction of three 3s in left-path coordinates
steps: For B=C=3, C₂(3)=4/3. The right-path intermediates F=6,3̄ have C₂=10/3,4/3, respectively.
Thus O_R/κ=diag(1/3,−2/3). Here κ may have either sign; its physical meaning is specified by the model.
Using the previous lesson's F, multiply out O_L/κ=[[-5/12,√3/4],[√3/4,1/12]] directly; nonzero off-diagonal entries appear.
The initial L₆ state has expectation −5κ/12. Weighting the right probabilities 1/4 and 3/4 likewise gives κ[(1/4)(1/3)+(3/4)(−2/3)]=−5κ/12.
example.result: Recoupling expresses the same two-body operator in another path basis. The matrix changes while physical expectation values remain the same.

lessons.pitfall: Transforming states without transforming operators changes the calculated expectation value. Racah  change of basis  alone specifies no Hamiltonian, coupling constant, or evolution time.

lessons.title: 24 · Fourfold  tensor product : pairing trees, crossings, and three levels of path labels
lessons.summary: Expand the (AB)(CD) and (AC)(BD) paths in the same A,B,C,D order and compare the copy spaces of the final representation.
objectives: Distinguish pair regrouping from particle exchange and apply the ACBD→ABCD permutation correctly
Retain the three  outer multiplicity  indices at both leaf vertices and the root vertex
Determine the size of R from the four-factor decomposition and path count

sections.title: Start from two pairs of factors
paragraphs: Four fixed, labeled representations A, B, C, D may couple AB and CD first, or AC and BD first. The left tree is ((A⊗B)E⊗(C⊗D)F)T and the right tree is ((A⊗C)G⊗(B⊗D)H)T. Denote the final type by T to avoid confusion with the third input C. Every binary tree has three binary vertices; labeling only two intermediate representations is insufficient.

In a left path ℓ=(E,α;F,β;γ), α labels copies in AB→E, β labels copies in CD→F, and γ labels copies in E_F→T. A right path r=(G,δ;H,ε;ζ) corresponds to the AC, BD and GH vertices. Whenever outer multiplicity occurs at a vertex, every combination must be retained as a separate path.

ℓ=(E,α:AB→E；F,β:CD→F；γ:E_F→T)
r=(G,δ:AC→G；H,ε:BD→H；ζ:GH→T)
m_T=Σ_(E,F) N_AB^E N_CD^F N_EF^T
   =Σ_(G,H) N_AC^G N_BD^H N_GH^T

sections.title: Crossed lines require a common tensor order
paragraphs: The left tree naturally gives coordinates in A⊗B⊗C⊗D and the right tree in A⊗C⊗B⊗D. Before taking overlaps, restore the latter to ABCD order with an explicit permutation P: P|a,c,b,d⟩=|a,b,c,d⟩. This rearrangement of tensor coordinates is valid even when B and C have different dimensions; omitting it incorrectly multiplies different product states entry by entry.

P compares two bases for the same labeled factors; it does not automatically supply a fermionic minus sign. A complete wavefunction of identical particles also requires the appropriate symmetrization or antisymmetrization across color, orbital, spin and other factors. This experiment calculates only pairing recoupling within the specified representation space.

sections.title: Isotypic subspaces, path multiplicities, and resource limits
paragraphs: For a fixed internal GT state μ of T, each side has m_T paths. Both embeddings obey the same SU(3)  intertwining relation , so R is independent of μ. The transformation of the complete T  isotypic subspace  is R⊗I_(dim T). R's size follows the path  multiplicity , neither the eight  generator  of SU(3) nor the product of the four input dimensions.

External factors may be any of the 15 types satisfying p+q≤4, including 10,15,15′,24,27 and their conjugates; the total four-factor product dimension must satisfy N≤4096. The final T is selected from the actual decomposition and may have labels outside the single-input range; dimension shorthand alone must not be used to filter it. Matrices, exact amplitudes, path labels, direction and conventions can be exported together. Exact expressions are constructed from integers, rational numbers and radicals.
sections.formula:
R†R=RR†=I_(m_T)
T isotypic subspace ≃ ℂ^(m_T)⊗V_T
N=dim A·dim B·dim C·dim D

example.title: Why do four 3 factors have three paths to the final 15?
steps: 3⊗3=6⊕3̄; in both trees the intermediate leaf representations may be 6 or 3̄.
For T=(2,1), (6,6), (6,3̄), and (3̄,6) each contribute once; (3̄,3̄) contributes nothing, so m_T=3.
The full decomposition is 3⁴=(4,0)⊕3·(2,1)⊕2·(0,2)⊕3·(1,0), with dimension check 81=15+45+12+9. The specified (2,1)  isotypic subspace  has dimension 45 and R is 3×3.
example.result: The equally dimensional (4,0) and (2,1) are 15′ and 15, respectively; here recoupling acts only among three copies of the specified (2,1).

lessons.title: 25 · Exact 9j coefficients: a 3×3 matrix from four product states
lessons.summary: Construct exact paths from highest-weight conditions and pair-exchange symmetries, then distinguish unitary recoupling R from the dimension-reduced 9j table S.
objectives: Independently derive all overlaps for four 3s coupled to 15
Clarify the relation among 9-U(3), the unitary matrix R and this project's dimension-reduced S
Prove dimension-weighted 9j orthogonality without confusing it with ordinary unitarity

sections.title: A three-dimensional  highest weight  space within a four-dimensional  weight space
paragraphs: Let x₁=|d,u,u,u⟩, x₂=|u,d,u,u⟩, x₃=|u,u,d,u⟩ and x₄=|u,u,u,d⟩. Their total weight is (H₁,H₂)=(2,1). E₁₂ sends every xᵢ to |u,u,u,u⟩, while E₂₃ annihilates them. The four coefficients of a (2,1) highest-weight vector must therefore sum to zero, leaving exactly three dimensions.

For path order (6,6), (6,3̄), (3̄,6), specify eigenvalues of both pair exchanges. Then select the following vectors with the binary CG GT phases. Right paths have already been restored from ACBD to common ABCD order, and each complete path is normalized.

sections.title: Evaluate nine exact inner products
paragraphs: Orthonormality of the xᵢ directly gives R_(rℓ)=⟨R_r|L_ℓ⟩. For example, R₁₁=(1−1−1+1)/4=0, R₁₂=1/√2 and R₂₂=1/2. A zero entry results from cancellation of signed amplitudes, not the absence of the entire final-15 channel.

In this example the matrix is real symmetric and obeys R²=I, a property of the identical inputs and current path conventions. The general inverse is still written R†. Reordering paths or changing complete-path phases changes whole rows or columns; transform external tables consistently before comparing them.

sections.title: Explicit definition of dimension-reduced 9j
paragraphs: The 9-U(3) coefficients in section V.2 of the reference paper connect unit-normalized paired states, serving the role of the unitary overlap matrix R here. To provide another 9j representation, this project additionally defines S_(rℓ)=R_(rℓ)/√[dim E_ℓ dim F_ℓ dim G_r dim H_r], retaining outer multiplicities at all three vertices and GT phases. S is not the unconverted numerical table of the paper's equation (30).

Let W_L=diag(dim E_ℓ dim F_ℓ) and W_R=diag(dim G_r dim H_r). Then R=W_R^(1/2) S W_L^(1/2), so unitarity of R gives S†W_R S=W_L⁻¹. State coordinates and probabilities use R; squared moduli of S generally have no such interpretation. Here W_L=W_R=diag(36,18,18), and all entries of S happen to be rational.

example.title: Cancellation and probabilities for the left (6,6) path
steps: Input a=(1,0,0)ᵀ, fixing final T=(2,1) and the same internal state.
The first column gives b=(0,1/√2,1/√2)ᵀ. The right (6,6) amplitude vanishes, while the other two probabilities are each 1/2.
The dimension-reduced coefficients of this column are (0,1/36,1/36)ᵀ, with weighted norm 18/36²+18/36²=1/36.
Recover a using R†b. Incorrectly using S gives a nonunit output norm, showing that the dimension-reduced table cannot directly replace the state-basis transformation matrix.
example.result: Exact R contains square roots, while exact S is rational in this example. Their definitions, orthogonality weights, and uses should accompany the results.

lessons.pitfall: A SU(3) table with nine representation labels additionally needs all  outer multiplicity , conjugation, and  phase convention  conventions. Replacing SU(2) j values with (p, q) in the same formula is invalid.
