lessons.title: 26 · Physical uses of four-body recoupling: color pairings, operators and complex phases
lessons.summary: Compare different color-space pairings while retaining exact complex amplitudes, and use the same R to transform two-body operators.
objectives: Distinguish color-pairing bases from complete many-particle dynamics
Identify the distinct origins of repeated copies at leaf branches and the root vertex
Keep complex phases for exact round trips and transform pair operators

sections.title: Color pairing is a basis choice in representation space
paragraphs: Take A,C as 3 and B,D as 3̄, in factor order 3⊗3̄⊗3⊗3̄. The left tree first forms two quark–antiquark pairs, each in 1 or 8; the right tree first forms 6 or 3̄ from the two 3 factors and 6̄ or 3 from the two 3̄ factors. This provides a color-space setting for rearranging meson-like and diquark-like pairings. Spatial, spin and flavor degrees of freedom are not included, nor are binding energies or hadronic reaction probabilities calculated.

For final T=1, the left paths are (8,8)→1 and (1,1)→1, and the right paths are (6,6̄)→1 and (3̄,3)→1, so m_1=2. For T=8, left (8,8)→8 has two root-vertex copies; adding (8,1) and (1,8) gives m_8=4. On the right, (6,6̄), (6,3), (3̄,6̄), and (3̄,3) each contribute once, again giving four paths. A final-octet block can describe a nonsinglet-color subsystem; it is not the color state of an isolated hadron.

sections.title: Repeated copies may occur at different vertices
paragraphs: For 8⊗8⊗1⊗1→8, the left tree already has two AB→8 copies, the exchange-symmetric 8s and antisymmetric 8a, followed by unique 8⊗1→8 coupling. In the right tree, AC→8 and BD→8 are unique, while the final 8⊗8→8 has two copies. Each tree has two paths, but the copy labels occur at different levels; a single ambiguous '8 channel' label is insufficient.

If an external factor is the trivial representation 1, its unique leaf branch can be removed for a cross-check against triple Racah recoupling. Tree shape, factor order, GT phases, and all path copies must still match; the presence of a 1 does not make two matrices with unaligned orderings equal entry by entry.

sections.title: Transform complex amplitudes and two-body operators together
paragraphs: For the four-3 block T=(2,1), take a=(1,i,0)ᵀ/√2 on the left. This project's R has real radical entries, but states can carry complex phases. Right coordinates b=(i/2,1/2+i√2/4,1/2−i√2/4)ᵀ give probabilities 1/4,3/8,3/8. Only multiplying the complete exact b by R† recovers the original phases.

If the model's two-body term is O=κΣₐTₐ^(A)Tₐ^(C), it is diagonal in the right tree according to the Casimir of intermediate G, ε_G=κ[C₂(G)−C₂(A)−C₂(C)]/2. Transforming to the left tree uses O_L=R†O_RR and preserves a†O_La=b†O_Rb. The particular model separately specifies κ and the Hamiltonian. The interactive experiment provides  recoupling  matrices and states; the operator application below is a worked example on paper.

example.title: The same A–C two-body term in another coupling tree
steps: With four 3 inputs, C₂(3)=4/3. The three right paths have G=6,6,3̄ and Casimirs 10/3,10/3,4/3.
Hence O_R/κ=diag(1/3,1/3,−2/3). Conjugate by the previous lesson's exact R:  change of basis .
O_L/κ=[[-1/6,√2/4,−√2/4],[√2/4,1/12,1/4],[−√2/4,1/4,1/12]]. Its off-diagonal entries show that left paths do not diagonalize the A–C pair interaction.
The pure left (6,6) state has expectation −κ/6. Right probabilities (0,1/2,1/2) give κ[0+(1/2)(1/3)+(1/2)(−2/3)]=−κ/6, agreeing with the left basis.
example.result: recoupling  changes path coordinates and operator matrices. Consistent  change of basis  preserves norms, projections, and expectation values. Recombining color bases alone does not specify dynamics.

lessons.pitfall: Color-channel weights depend on the specified state and pairing basis. They are not directly reaction cross sections, model-independent probabilities of bound-state components, or the full statistical symmetry of identical particles.

lessons.title: 27 · From 4096 dimensions to multiplicity blocks: complete channels of four octets
lessons.summary: Decompose 8⊗8⊗8⊗8 into 13 final types, distinguishing total space, isotypic subspaces, and path spaces of dimensions 8,32,33.
objectives: Count fourfold paths using the  outer multiplicity  of all three vertices
Check all 13 final types in 8⁴ and their dimension sum
Independently check high-dimensional recoupling blocks using exchange-operator traces

sections.title: Three different dimensions
paragraphs: Every external factor is the adjoint 8=(1,1), so the total space has dimension 8⁴=4096. For fixed final type T, its occurrence count m_T is the path-space dimension, while its isotypic subspace has dimension m_T·dim(T). For example, T=8 has 32 paths and a 256-dimensional isotypic subspace, with R of size 32×32; T=27 has 33 paths and dimension 891, with R of size 33×33. The final singlet has eight paths and an 8×8 R matrix.

The full decomposition contains 13 distinct final irreducible types. Numerical coefficients below are outer multiplicities. Conjugate types such as 81 and 81̄, or 35 and 35̄, have equal dimensions but different Dynkin labels. The largest output (4,4) has dimension 125 and may exceed the label range allowed for a single input.

sections.title: Both copies of 8 occur independently in the two leaf branches
paragraphs: Every leaf pair satisfies 8⊗8=27⊕10⊕10̄⊕2·8⊕1. A left-tree path is (E,α;F,β;γ): α and β select copies on the two leaf branches, while γ selects a copy at the root E⊗F→T. The right-tree labels are (G,δ;H,ε;ζ). These three indices cannot be merged into a single 'octet copy' label.

For a final singlet, only F=Ē occurs and the root vertex is unique. Types 27,10,10̄,1 each contribute once. For E=F=8, both α and β have two choices, contributing four paths and giving eight in total. Thus E=F=8 does not specify a unique path. For final T=8, the (8,8) branch also has two root copies, giving 2×2×2=8 paths. For final T=27, the (27,27) branch has three root copies, two symmetric and one antisymmetric. Retain root labels independently.

sections.title: Identical factors provide independent exchange checks
paragraphs: With four identical external factors and matching binary GT conventions, copies, and path ordering, crossed pairing is exchange of the middle factors B,C in common ABCD coordinates. This permutation P₂₃ obeys P₂₃†=P₂₃ and P₂₃²=I, so exact R should be a real symmetric involution. This is an additional symmetry of this example; general mixed-factor R is treated as unitary.

The numbers of positive and negative exchange eigenstates can be calculated independently from symmetric and antisymmetric decompositions of the BC pair. Sym²8=27⊕8s⊕1, Λ²8=10⊕10̄⊕8a. Coupling with the remaining 8⊗8 gives (n₊,n₋)=(4,4), (16,16), and (17,16) in the T=1, 8, and 27 path spaces, respectively. These trace checks require no prior knowledge of specific CG radicals.

example.title: The 33 paths to a final 27 and their exchange eigenvalues
steps: Fixing the first leaf pair to E=27,10,10̄,8,1 and summing over the second pair F gives contributions 10,5,5,12,1, already including leaf-branch copies.
Total  multiplicity  m_27=10+5+5+12+1=33; the final  isotypic subspace  has dimension 33×27=891, while the full fourfold space remains 4096-dimensional.
For the positive BC-exchange subspace, restrict E to 27,8s,1, obtaining n₊=10+12/2+1=17. The negative subspace comes from 10,10̄,8a, giving n₋=5+5+12/2=16.
The 33×33 R therefore has 17 eigenvalues +1 and 16 eigenvalues −1, with tr R=1 and R²=I. Its entries still require exact coupling calculations; counting alone does not determine every coefficient.
example.result: R's order is determined by  outer multiplicity . The numbers 4096, 891, and 33 answer three different questions: total dimension, isotypic dimension of the final 27, and path dimension.

lessons.pitfall: 8³→8 has exactly eight paths, as does 8⁴→1, but the factor count, final representation and trees differ. Two 8×8 matrices need not have the same coefficients.

lessons.title: 28 · Four-octet singlets: independently check 9j using δ invariants
lessons.summary: Start with two normalized adjoint singlets and directly obtain the crossed-singlet amplitude 1/8 and probabilities aggregated by representation.
objectives: Derive exact crossed-pairing amplitudes from invariant tensors
Obtain aggregated probabilities for each representation using reduced  density matrix

sections.title: Write the singlet in a real orthonormal adjoint basis
paragraphs: The adjoint representation 8 admits a real orthogonal Cartesian basis, with indices a, b, c, d=1,…,8. The normalized two-factor singlet is δ_{ab}/√8. The left product of two singlets χ_L=δ_{ab}δ_{cd}/8 and the right crossed singlet χ_R=δ_{ac}δ_{bd}/8 are both in the common ABCD order. Their root vertex is the unique 1⊗1→1.

Both tensors are final-T=1 states. In their inner product, the four δ factors require a=b=c=d, leaving eight terms; the overlap is therefore 8/64=1/8, and the probability of the crossed double singlet is 1/64. This diagonal overlap does not change sign under rephasing of the same pairing basis; entrywise signs elsewhere still require this project's GT convention.

sections.title: Total probabilities for other color channels do not require guessing coefficients
paragraphs: χ_L is a product of maximally  entanglement  AB and CD singlets. Tracing out B and D leaves reduced AC  density matrix  ρ_AC=I₆₄/64. The total probability of an irreducible type G in AC is therefore the rank of its isotypic projector divided by 64. Type 8 occurs twice, with total projector rank 2×8=16.

Aggregate the right output by Dynkin label G to obtain 27/64,10/64,10/64,16/64,1/64, summing to 1. The 16/64 is the total probability over all G=8 paths. Phases and distributions of particular copies must be checked against the actual path convention; aggregated values cannot be assigned directly to every '8' entry.

sections.title: Exact eight-path table and weighted orthogonality
paragraphs: The singlet block's intermediate types can be listed as (27,27), (10,10̄), (10̄,10), four (8,8) paths, and (1,1). Each path also carries copy labels at all three vertices. Their dimension products are 729, 100, 100, four 64s, and 1. The interface displays full labels in current path order and offers R or this project's dimension-reduced S.

Since S=W_R^(−1/2)RW_L^(−1/2), S cannot be treated as an ordinary unitary matrix even when m=8. For the input double-singlet column, its W_L entry is 1 and the weighted norm is Σ_r W_R,rr |S_rℓ|²=1. The double-singlet diagonal entry happens to have no additional dimension scaling, S_ℓℓ=R_ℓℓ=1/8; this special case does not extend to the whole table.

example.title: Obtain five aggregated probabilities from one definite left path
steps: Choose four 8 factors, a final singlet and the pure left (E,F)=(1,1) path. Its normalized Cartesian amplitude is δ_{ab}δ_{cd}/8.
Contracting four δ tensors for crossed double singlets leaves eight nonzero terms, giving amplitude 1/8 and probability 1/64.
Taking the reduced AC  density matrix  gives I₆₄/64. Trace it against projectors of dimensions 27, 10, 10, 16, and 1.
The five probabilities are 27/64,5/32,5/32,1/4,1/64 and sum to 1. Aggregate all experimental right paths by their first intermediate type G to check them individually.
example.result: One diagonal coefficient and the probabilities of five channel types can be checked independently without a CG table; the experiment also provides every exact entry with copy and phase labels.

lessons.pitfall: Cartesian invariants are representation coordinates convenient for hand calculation; the experiment uses GT coordinates. Vectors can be compared entry by entry only after transforming to the same basis. Total projection probabilities and inner products remain invariant.

sections.title: Casimir energy levels of an adjoint pair
paragraphs: Consider the SU(3)-invariant model term O=κΣₐTₐ^(A)Tₐ^(C), with Casimir normalization Tₐ=λₐ/2 and C₂(p,q)=(p²+q²+pq+3p+3q)/3. Both external adjoint factors have C₂(8)=3, so the operator is diagonal by G in the right tree, with ε_G=κ[C₂(G)−6]/2.

The energies of G=27, 10, 10̄, 8, and 1 are κ, 0, 0, −3κ/2, and −3κ. Copies of the same type share this two-body Casimir energy but remain distinct paths. Transform to the left tree with O_L=R†O_RR; expectations a†O_La and b†O_Rb must agree.

sections.title: The four-adjoint color model and its computational scope
paragraphs: The adjoint representation describes gluon color degrees of freedom, so pairing four adjoint factors illustrates regrouping of multigluon color bases. This classroom constructs labeled factors, paths, and projectors in representation space only. It specifies neither orbitals, polarizations, complete identical-boson permutation constraints, nor QCD dynamics. Final nonsinglet blocks can represent subsystem channels of a larger color system.

The exact fourfold experiment now accepts all 15 external p+q≤4 types, including 10, 15, 15′, 24, 27, and their conjugates, subject to total four-factor N≤4096. Every fourfold combination of the original six p+q≤2 factors remains included, including 8⁴; four 27s or four 10s exceed the total-dimension limit. Final types come from the actual decomposition and are not truncated by single-input label limits. Triple Racah and binary CG retain their own limits. Exact algebra with high  multiplicity  can take time on first use; subsequent calculations in the same kernel reuse completed coupling data.

example.title: Mean and fluctuations of a double singlet in a crossed two-body model
steps: The left double singlet χ_L has right-channel aggregated probabilities (27,10,10,16,1)/64 for G=27, 10, 10̄, 8, and 1.
Substituting Casimir energies gives ⟨O⟩/κ=[27×1+10×0+10×0+16×(−3/2)+1×(−3)]/64=0.
A zero mean does not make the state a zero-eigenvalue eigenstate of O. Squaring gives ⟨O²⟩/κ²=[27+16×9/4+9]/64=9/8.
The variance is therefore 9κ²/8. Conjugating O_R into left-path coordinates and recalculating must give the same mean and variance, providing a check independent of individual entry signs.
example.result: Higher-dimensional recoupling preserves normalization, expectation values and fluctuations. The operator on paper is defined by the chosen model; changing color coordinates alone does not determine reaction cross sections or binding energies.

lessons.pitfall: Replacing R by dimension-reduced S in state or operator transformations breaks norm or expectation-value preservation. Display decimals also cannot replace complete exact complex amplitudes in reverse transformations.

objectives: Distinguish equal-dimensional 15, 15̄, 15′, and 15̄′; do not select representations by dimension alone

sections.title: Dimension does not uniquely name a SU(3) representation
paragraphs: An SU(3) irreducible representation is specified by nonnegative integers (p,q); conjugation exchanges the labels. 10=(3,0) and 10̄=(0,3) are different types. 15=(2,1),15̄=(1,2),15′=(4,0),15̄′=(0,4) all have dimension 15 but are not the same representation. 27=(2,2) is self-conjugate. The interface displays names together with full labels, and every exact calculation uses the labels.

With Tₐ=λₐ/2, representations 15 and 15′ have Casimirs 16/3 and 28/3, respectively; their equal dimensions do not make them interchangeable. Conjugate types share a Casimir but have distinct weights and tensor products.

sections.title: With 10 as an input, the final 15 occurs four times
paragraphs: A calculable preset takes A=10,B=3,C=3,D=3̄, with all four factors nontrivial. The total dimension is N=10×3×3×3=270. Fixing T=15=(2,1) gives four paths, a 4×15=60-dimensional isotypic subspace and a 4×4 unitary R. Here 10 is an external leaf and the final 15 is at the root, unlike merely coupling lower-dimensional inputs to a higher-dimensional output.

Both AB and AC decompose as 10⊗3=15′⊕15, and the other pair as 3⊗3̄=8⊕1. Final 15 receives one path from (15,1), two root copies from (15,8), and one from (15′,8), totaling four. The roles of 15 and 15′ differ, and (15,8) must not be counted only once.

sections.title: Another decuplet example: S₃ gives exact probabilities
paragraphs: Choose the 10⊗3⊗3⊗3→8 interactive preset. Here m_8=2, with the CD pair in symmetric 6 or antisymmetric 3̄. The three fundamental factors B,C,D decompose as 3³=10⊕2·8⊕1; only the two 8 copies combine with A=10 to give final 8. This two-dimensional path space therefore carries the standard representation of S₃.

CD exchange is D=diag(1,−1) on symmetric and antisymmetric paths; BC exchange produces a real symmetric involution R. A three-cycle requires (DR)³=I and has trace −1 in the standard representation. R therefore has diagonal magnitudes 1/2 and off-diagonal magnitudes √3/2. Basis phases can change some signs, but not the 1/4 and 3/4 probabilities between these two paths already distinguished by CD exchange.

example.title: Why are the two fifteen-dimensional types not interchangeable?
steps: Substitute (2,1) and (4,0) into the dimension formula to obtain 3×2×5/2=15 and 5×1×6/2=15.
Each occurs once in 10⊗3=15′⊕15. On coupling to 8 with final T=(2,1), the former contributes once and the latter twice.
Read each path's (p, q) and root copy γ rather than merging all representations labeled “15.” Exact exports retain these labels.
example.result: Equal dimensions do not imply equal representations. The four-path example with input 10 and final 15 directly exposes the differences among 15,15′ and root-vertex outer multiplicity.

lessons.pitfall: N≤4096 bounds the total product dimension, not each factor independently. 10⁴=10000 and 27⁴=531441 exceed the current limit. A high-dimensional output must not be confused with having used that same type as an input.

Distinguish path rephasing, rotations of outer-multiplicity space, and representation-type projections

sections.title: First count five paths along AB and CD
paragraphs: Take A=15=(2,1),B=3,C=3̄,D=3 and final T=24=(3,1). AB decomposes as 24⊕15̄⊕6 and CD as 8⊕1. Each leaf-branch type appears once, so α and β are unique, but the root vertex may still have repeated copies.

Final 24 receives one path from (24,1), two root copies from (24,8), one from (15̄,8), and one from (6,8), totaling five. N=405, the final-24 isotypic space has dimension 120, and R is 5×5. Complete path labels distinguish γ=1,2 for (24,8).

sections.title: Follow AC and BD instead and count the same five paths
paragraphs: AC decomposes as 15⊗3̄=27⊕10⊕8 and BD as 3⊗3=6⊕3̄. Right paths to final 24 are (27,6), (27,3̄), (10,6), (10,3̄), and (8,6), each with a unique root vertex. The five left and five right paths are distinct orthonormal bases, not one-to-one matches of identical intermediate labels.

Construct the right tree in ACBD order, permute to ABCD, then calculate R=V_R†V_L. C has type 3̄ and B has type 3. This example requires neither a symmetric R nor R²=I; the general inverse is R†. Equal path counts follow from  tensor product  associativity, independently of R's particular radicals.

sections.title: Record phases and copy bases together with the matrix
paragraphs: This project chooses its own GT phases and orthogonal copy bases at binary vertices. Rephasing complete left or right paths changes phases of the corresponding columns or rows of R; general unitary rotations among repeated copies of the same type mix entries. Before comparing with external tables entry by entry, align representation labels, factor order,  outer multiplicity  bases, and phases.

Write new path bases as V_LU_L,V_RU_R. Then R′=U_R†RU_L and state coordinates must also change to a′=U_L†a. Consistent transformations of the same physical state preserve norms and physical projections. Rotating repeated copies generally changes individual-copy probabilities; projection probabilities summed over a definite intermediate type remain invariant under rotations within that type.

The total space is N=27×3×3×3=729; the final 42 occurs five times, its  isotypic subspace  has dimension 210, and the exact  recoupling  matrix is 5×5. Final label p+q=5 exceeds the range of single-input p+q≤4, but occurs in the decomposition and must remain selectable.
